newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen soldier kills at least seven on election day.
newsitem.headline: Yemen soldier kills at least seven on election day.

text.p: A Yemeni official said on Sunday that seven people were killed when a soldier opened fire at a polling station before voting started on Sunday in the country's first general election since a 1994 civil war.

"Seven people were killed when a soldier on night duty opened fire at the polling station (in southern Yemen)," Saeed al-Hekaimi, spokesman for the Supreme Election Committee told a news conference in the capital Sanaa.
"It is a criminal act...Investigations are under way," he added.
A Security source put the death toll from the dawn attack in the town of Mukayras in the governorate of Abyan at eight.
One of the victims was a member of Yemen's ruling party -- the General Peoples Congress (GPC), the source told Reuters. He said two people were also injured in the attack.

"The soldier opened fire on them while they were sleeping in their room before the polling station opened," a security official said earlier. He said the soldier was arrested and authorities were trying to determine why he carried out the attack, the third fatal assault in the run-up to the poll.

Military police in red berets stood guard as voters, who included elderly men with traditional curved daggers tucked in their belts and women in black veils, began voting at 8.00 a.m. (0500 GMT) in a race they hope will guarantee enough stability to lure foreign funds into the poor Arab state.
It is the first ballot since the 1994 civil war. Polling stations are due to close at 6.00 p.m. (1500 GMT).

President Ali Abdullah Saleh cast his ballot along with many of Yemen's 4.6 million eligible voters who are choosing from among 2,306 candidates, including 17 women, competing for 301 seats under the banner of 12 parties or as independents.
Minor scuffles were reported at several Sanaa polling stations, but international observers said the election process appeared to be going well so far.
Diplomats and some observers said there could be trouble in the governorates of Ibb and Taiz, where bloody tribal politics have previously mixed with the election race.

A Yemeni man was killed in Ibb on April 20 when armed clashes broke out between supporters of Saleh's GPC and backers of its junior coalition partner, the Islamist Islah Party. A child was also killed in Taiz on Thursday when gunmen opened fire on a GPC rally.

One election monitor said a decision by the Supreme Election Committee late on Saturday to let 1.4 million registered Yemeni voters cast their ballot even though they had not picked up permanent election cards had raised concerns among some parties.
"There are concerns among some parties that this could lead to manipulation of voting," one observer said.
Voters, many of them illiterate, made their choice with the help of ballot slips bearing the symbols of parties -- from horses and camels to candles and rockets.
Diplomats expect Saleh's GPC and Islah to win a majority.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party, some of whose former leaders launched the separatist campaign that sparked the civil war, and three others are boycotting the polls due to alleged irregularities. The government has denied the charges.
Results are expected to start trickling in on Monday afternoon, but final results are only due later in the week.

Diplomats say they are encouraged by Yemen's democratic experiment but add that power ultimately rests in the hands of the president, appointed ministers, the military and security forces loyal to the GPC.
"If you look at the past parliament, it was really a tiger with no teeth. It is more of a pressure group," said one.
They said the government was trying to boost its democratic image abroad to attract foreign investment and aid to Yemen.
The Republic of Yemen was formed in 1990 by the merger of the conservative North Yemen and the Marxist south.
